name: Kokkos
baseline: OpenMP (hand-written OpenMP variant of the same particle-in-cell plasma code)
workload: Particle movement rate of a particle-in-cell plasma physics code ported to Kokkos versus its OpenMP variant, on server CPUs.
claimed_speedup: Kokkos particle movement rate 1.4x the OpenMP variant on Kabre's Intel Xeon Gold 6354, 1.6x on Raven's Intel Xeon Platinum 8360Y; performance-portability metric 100% (Kokkos) vs 67% (OpenMP) (snippet only, paper not opened)
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6354 (Kabre); Intel Xeon Platinum 8360Y (Raven); the paper also used AMD EPYC CPUs and NVIDIA and AMD GPUs
stars_or_usage: 2.7k stars; Linux Foundation / HPSF established project
tradeoffs: Performance-portability programming model (CUDA, HIP, SYCL, HPX, OpenMP and C++ threads backends), not a drop-in thread pool; requires C++20; code must be written against Kokkos Views and parallel dispatch.
caveats: Snippet only: arxiv.org is blocked in this environment, so the numbers come from a web search summary of 'A Study of Performance Portability in Plasma Physics Simulations' (CARLA 2024 submission) and could not be checked against the paper; compiler, flags and benchmark code were not seen. The comparison is application-level (one PIC code, a Kokkos port against its own OpenMP variant, where Kokkos's automatic memory layout is credited), not a Kokkos-versus-OpenMP micro benchmark, so it says little about Kokkos's scheduler. Other third-party studies in the same search report Kokkos overheads of 13-18% (ocean model, CPU) and about 70% of native CUDA throughput (CMS pixel reconstruction), so Kokkos is not generally faster than native code. The repo's own core/perf_test and benchmarks/ directories (stream, gups, launch_latency, atomic, ...) publish no result tables. last_commit not read (github.com commits page returned HTTP 429); maintenance 'active' is from the README naming release 5.1.0 as current and the CI badges.
